1. e4 {The king's pawn, two moves.} e5 {The same.} 2. Bc4 {The king's bishop, at his queen's
bishop's fourth square.} Bc5 {The same.} 3. c3 {The queen's bishop's pawn, one move.} Nf6 {The
king's knight, at his bishop's third square.} 4. d4 {The queen's pawn, two moves, (a) NOTE: You
might push this pawn only one move; but then your situation would be the same as that already
shewed in the first variable.} exd4 {The king's pawn takes the pawn.} 5. cxd4 {The queen's
bishop's pawn retakes the pawn. (b) NOTE: Instead of taking, you might push the king's pawn one
move. This would be a very good move against a player to whom advantage is granted. The subject
of a back game.} Bb4+ {The king's bishop gives check. (c) NOTE: The first part of the former
edition proves, that, by the removal of this bishop to his queen's knight's third square, the
adversary is set at liberty to establish his pawns in the centre,} 6. Bd2 {The queen's bishop
covers the check.} Bxd2+ {The king's bishop takes the bishop.} 7. Nxd2 {The queen's knight
retakes the bishop.} d5 {The queen's pawn, two moves. (d) NOTE: Had he not made this move, he
would have given you time to occupy the centre with your pawns: the advantage derived from this,
is sufficiently proved, as well in the former, as in this edition.} 8. exd5 {The king's pawn
takes the pawn.} Nxd5 {The king's knight retakes the pawn.} 9. Qb3 {The queen, at her knight's
third square. (e) NOTE: It is in your power to give check with your queen at your king's second
square; but by this move your adversary would be impowered to get out his queen's bishop:
besides, the queen and king are never to be placed on the same line, when that is opened and
unguarded by the pawns.} c6 {The queen's bishop's pawn, one move.} 10. Ne2 {The king's knight,
at his king's second square.} O-O {The king castles.} 11. O-O {The king castles with his rook.}
Nb6 {The king's knight, at his queen's knight's third square. (f) NOTE: He plays this knight
with a design, either to get out his queen's bishop, or to get rid of your king's bishop.} 12.
Bd3 {The king's bishop, at his queen's third square.} Be6 {The queen's bishop, at his king's
third square.} 13. Qc2 {The queen, at her bishop's second square.} g6 {The king's knight's pawn,
one move.} 14. f4 {The king's bishop's pawn, two moves. (g) NOTE: You push this pawn, to break
the chain of the pawns that cover his king.} f5 {The same. (h) 15.1 NOTE: As he has pushed his
king's bishop's pawn two moves, you must strive to post one of your knights at the adverse
king's fourth square. From that place he cannot be driven out by any piece, unless he be taken,
and then you may re-unite your pawns in the cen tre...} 15. Nf3 {The queen's knight, at his
king's bishop's third square.} N8d7 {The queen's knight, at his queen's second square.} 16. Ne5
{The queen's knight, at the adverse king's fourth square.} Nf6 {The queen's knight, at his
king's bishop's third square.. (i) NOTE: He will not re-unite your pawns by tak ng your knight.}
17. Rad1 {The queen's rook, at its queen's square.} Nbd5 {The king's knight, at his queen's
fourth square.} 18. Qd2 {The queen, at her second square. (k) NOTE: This move is necessary, to
hinder his knight from taking his place at your king's third square.} a5 {The queen's rook's
pawn, two moves.} 19. Nc3 {The king's knight, at his queen's bishop's third square. (l) NOTE: In
these reciprocal positions, I should think, the white has the better game, on account of the
place where the queen's knight stands: nevertheless, this advantage is not of such consequence,
as to decide the game on that side. The black must be mindful, not to take the knight before
they have destroyed one of the pawns that sustain the knight, which may be done by changing the
queen's bishop's pawn with the adverse queen's pawn; and then both games will be quite even.} *
</script></div>
